headline: Healey urges faster federal review of New England gas pipeline expansion
dek: Project RARE would replace and add sections of Enbridge's Algonquin system in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, a proposal supporters tie to winter energy costs and critics say would prolong fossil-fuel dependence.
body: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey is asking the federal government to move faster on its review of a proposed natural-gas pipeline expansion that would reach into Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In a letter to U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Healey said the Reliable Affordable Resilient Enhancement project, known as Project RARE, could lower costs for about 600,000 customers. Her request does not approve the project: federal regulators are still in the pre-filing environmental-review stage.

The governor's letter is the latest turn in a regional argument over how to handle New England's high winter energy costs. Healey's administration says constrained gas supply on the coldest days can push power plants toward more expensive oil and force utilities to buy liquefied natural gas. The administration is asking for a timely review while saying environmental review and community engagement should continue. The Massachusetts announcement is at https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-calls-on-trump-administration-to-expedite-review-of-gas-pipeline-expansion.

Project RARE is being developed by Enbridge along its Algonquin natural-gas system, which runs from New Jersey through New York and southern New England. WBUR reported that the proposal would replace about eight miles of existing pipe with larger-diameter pipe in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, add a parallel section in Rhode Island and upgrade a compressor station in Cromwell, Connecticut. Enbridge has said the expansion would add roughly 75 million cubic feet per day of capacity. WBUR's report is at https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/01/governor-healey-project-rare-natural-gas-pipeline-expansion-fossil-fuels-climate.

Federal records provide a more detailed picture of the footprint. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission says the planned facilities total about 13.5 miles in Massachusetts and Rhode Island. The proposal includes replacing about 8.25 miles of 16-inch pipe with 36-inch pipe in Norfolk and Worcester counties and Providence County, Rhode Island; installing about 2.2 miles of 12-inch looping pipe in Newport County; and adding three miles of 36-inch looping pipe in Providence County. It also includes software-related compression changes at the Cromwell station. FERC's project page, docket PF26-7-000, says the project has not been approved: https://www.ferc.gov/Algonquin-Gas-Transmission-Enhancement-Project.

The local stakes extend beyond a construction map. FERC says the project is intended to increase supply to local distribution companies and improve regional reliability, while the Massachusetts administration and Eversource have connected new capacity to lower winter reliance on liquefied natural gas. WBUR reported that Massachusetts regulators approved a 10-year Eversource purchase plan tied to the expansion and that the state estimates it could reduce the utility's liquefied-natural-gas use by about $40 million annually. That estimate is a projected benefit, not a guaranteed reduction on a household bill.

The project is also colliding with Massachusetts' climate requirements and a broader fight over the role of gas in the regional grid. WBUR reported that climate advocates questioned whether adding pipeline capacity could lock in more gas use even if it reduces short-term reliance on liquefied natural gas. Conservation Law Foundation said Healey's request repeated a claim about lower heating costs that the group disputes, arguing that cleaner hydroelectric and offshore-wind deliveries have been the more reliable source of price containment. CLF's response is at https://www.clf.org/newsroom/clf-challenges-gas-pipeline-push/.

FERC's pre-filing process is not the final permitting decision. The agency describes it as a pre-application phase designed to surface environmental issues before an official application, with opportunities for public comments, open houses and scoping sessions. That means residents, landowners and communities along the proposed work areas still have a formal role as the record develops. The agency's page lists earlier 2026 open houses in Wrentham and Bellingham, Massachusetts, and in several Rhode Island communities; later filings and notices will determine the next steps.

For Massachusetts, the immediate question is whether faster federal attention produces a faster decision without narrowing the review. Healey is positioning Project RARE as one response to costly winter energy constraints, while environmental groups warn that the long-term answer must reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Until Enbridge files the project for full federal review and regulators evaluate its environmental and reliability claims, the expansion remains a proposal rather than new pipeline capacity. The review, and the debate over who should bear its costs and risks, now moves forward on two tracks.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts asks faster review of Project RARE gas pipeline
seoDescription: Gov. Maura Healey wants faster federal review of Project RARE, a proposed Enbridge gas-pipeline expansion in Massachusetts and Rhode Island.
